It is one of the candidate shrines ({{ill|Shikinai Ronsha|ja|論社|qid=Q135022904}}) for the {{ill|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|abstract|Q11064932|fr|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|ja|延喜式神名帳|simple|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|zh|延喜式神名帳|qid=Q11064932|lt=Shikinaisha}} “Nunakawa Shrine.” Its official name is '''Hakusan Shrine'''<ref>According to the list of shrines on the Niigata Prefecture Association of Shinto Shrines website.</ref>. {{nihongo|'''Nō Hakusan Shrine'''|能生白山神社}} is a [[shinto shrine]] in the [[Engishiki Jinmyōchō]]. It is located in [[Echigo Province]].

== Enshrined deities ==
The shrine enshrines {{ill|Nunakawahime|it|Nunakawahime|ja|沼河比売|zh|沼河比賣|qid=Q11142832|lt=Nunakawahime-no-Mikoto}}, {{ill|Izanagi|abstract|Q813858|ar|إزاناغي|az|İzanaqi|bcl|Izanagi|bn|ইজানাগি|bs|Izanagi|ca|Izanagi|cs|Izanagi a Izanami|da|Izanagi|el|Ιζανάγκι|eo|Izanagi|es|Izanagi|fa|ایزاناگی|fi|Izanaki|fr|Izanagi|he|איזאנגי|hr|Izanagi|hu|Izanagi|id|Izanagi|it|Izanagi|ja|イザナギ|ka|იძანაგი|ko|이자나기|lt|Idzanagis|mk|Изанаги|mni|ꯏꯓꯥꯅꯥꯒꯤ|no|Izanagi|or|ଇଜାନାଗି|pt|Izanagi|ro|Izanagi|rsk|Изанаґи|ru|Идзанаги|simple|Izanagi|sk|Izanagi|sl|Izanagi|sr|Изанаки|sv|Izanagi|ta|இசநாகி|th|อิซานางิ|tl|Izanagi|tr|İzanagi|uk|Ідзанаґі|vi|Izanagi|zh|伊邪那岐|qid=Q813858|lt=Izanagi-no-Mikoto}}, and {{ill|Ōkuninushi|lt=Ōnamuchi-no-Mikoto|qid=Q276944}}. Nunakawahime-no-Mikoto is a goddess who has long been worshipped throughout the region centered on Itoigawa City. She is known from the 『{{ill|Kojiki|ace|Kojiki|ar|كوجيكي|az|Kociki|bcl|Kojiki|be|Кодзікі|bg|Коджики|ca|Kojiki|ckb|کۆجیکی|cs|Kodžiki|da|Kojiki|de|Kojiki|eo|Koĝiki|es|Kojiki|et|Kojiki|eu|Kojiki|fa|کوجیکی|fi|Kojiki|fr|Kojiki|gl|Kojiki|he|קוג'יקי|hi|कोजिकी|hr|Kojiki|hu|Kodzsiki|hy|Կոձիկի|id|Kojiki|it|Kojiki|ja|古事記|ka|კოძიკი|kk|Кодзики|kn|ಕೋಜಿಕಿ|ko|고사기|la|Kojiki|lt|Kodžiki|mk|Коџики|ml|കൊജികി|ms|Kojiki|my|ခိုဂျိခိ|nl|Kojiki|no|Kojiki|oc|Kojiki|pl|Kojiki|pt|Kojiki|ro|Kojiki|rsk|Кодїки|ru|Кодзики|sh|Kojiki|simple|Kojiki|sk|Kodžiki|sl|Kodžiki|sr|Коџики|sv|Kojiki|ta|கோஜிகி|th|โคจิกิ|tl|Kojiki|tr|Kojiki|uk|Кодзікі|vi|Cổ sự ký|zh|古事記|zh_classical|古事記|qid=Q813031}}』 for her courtship and marriage with Ōkuninushi-no-Mikoto, as well as the story of moving to Shinano together for the governance of the land. In ancient times, the {{ill|Nishikubiki District, Niigata|ja|西頸城郡|ko|니시쿠비키군|qid=Q11629983}} area of Niigata Prefecture was known as Nunakawa-no-shō.

There are many legends and rituals related to Nunakawahime-no-Mikoto in the area surrounding Hakusan Shrine. In Ōaza Shimamichi within the city, slightly up the mountainside from the Shimamichi River (a tributary of the {{ill|Nou River|ja|能生川|qid=Q134567545}}, formerly said to be called Nunokawa), which flows from Mount Ōsawa, there is a large rock cave said to be the birthplace of Nunakawahime-no-Mikoto. Downstream in Omi is Omi Hakusan Shrine, whose enshrined deities are Izanagi-no-Mikoto, Ōnamuchi-no-Mikoto, and {{ill|Kikurihime|Q11619891|qid=Q11619891|lt=Kikurihime-no-Mikoto}}. According to the origin legend of Omi Hakusan Shrine, the cave is also said to have been the residence when Ōnamuchi-no-Mikoto married into the household of Nunakawahime-no-Mikoto of Koshi. Mount Ōsawa is connected to Shindōzan (Shindō-no-mine), which is passed down in legend as the path Ōkuninushi-no-Mikoto traveled to court Nunakawahime-no-Mikoto. There are 1,088 stone steps leading to the summit.

== History ==
According to a prewar “Prospectus of the Repair Donation Association,” the shrine is said to have been founded on the first Horse Day of the 11th month in the 11th year of {{ill|Emperor Sujin|Q333530|qid=Q333530}}.

During the reign of {{ill|Empress Genshō|ar|الإمبراطورة غينشو|arz|الامبراطوره جينشو|bcl|Emperatris Genshō|ca|Genshō|ckb|ئیمپراتۆر گێنشۆ|cs|Genšó|de|Genshō|es|Genshō Tennō|fa|امپراتریس گنشو|fi|Genshō|fr|Genshō|hu|Gensó japán császárnő|id|Genshō|it|Genshō|ja|元正天皇|ko|겐쇼 천황|la|Genshō (imperatrix)|mk|Царица Геншо|nl|Gensho|pl|Genshō|pt|Gensho|ru|Императрица Гэнсё|sh|Carica Genshō|simple|Empress Genshō|sl|Cesarica Genšo|sv|Genshō|ta|பேரரசி ஜென்ஷோ|th|จักรพรรดินีเก็นโช|tl|Emperatris Genshō|tr|Genshō (imparatoriçe)|uk|Імператор Ґенсьо|vi|Thiên hoàng Genshō|zh|元正天皇|zh_min_nan|Gensyô Thian-hông|qid=Q235343}}, the monk {{ill|Taichō|de|Taichō|fr|Taichō|it|Taichō|ja|泰澄|qid=Q2388439|lt=Taichō Daishi}} deeply revered the shrine, installed Buddhist statues, and named it “Hakusan Gongen.” In the {{ill|Kankō|Q2736722|qid=Q2736722}} era (early 11th century), a divided spirit was transferred from {{ill|Shirayama Hime Shrine|Q704702|qid=Q704702|lt=Kaga Hakusan Shrine}} and enshrined together at the former shrine site. Nouzan Taiheiji Hōkōin flourished as a subsidiary hall of Hakusan Gongen, at one time possessing a complex of seven halls, 75 subsidiary shrines, and more than 50 temple lodgings.

== Rituals ==
The “Nou Nunakawa Festival,” based on the long-told myths of Nunakawahime-no-Mikoto and Ōnamuchi-no-Mikoto, features a bridal procession, ancient threshing rites, rice-polishing rituals, and mochi pounding.

The Spring Grand Festival is held every year on April 24 and is locally known as the “Nou Festival.” Eleven pieces of bugaku and a lion dance are performed, and the final dance, “Ryōō no Mai,” is especially striking, with crimson costumes set against the evening sun of early spring. The bugaku was selected in {{ill|1973|Q2477|qid=Q2477}} (Shōwa 48) as a National {{ill|Intangible Folk Cultural Properties Requiring Documentation|Q11642584|qid=Q11642584}} (Selected Intangible Folk Cultural Property), and in 1980 (Shōwa 55) was designated as a National {{ill|National Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property|Q6573893|qid=Q6573893}} under the name “Nou Bugaku” (see also “{{ill|Itoigawa-No's Bugaku|Q11604877|qid=Q11604877}}” and “{{ill|Hakusan Shrine Bugaku|Q11579603|qid=Q11579603}}”).

== Shrine buildings ==
The main hall is a {{ill|Nagare-zukuri|fr|Nagare-zukuri|it|Nagare-zukuri|ja|流造|pl|Nagare-zukuri|ru|Нагарэ-дзукури|sv|Nagare-zukuri|zh|流造|qid=Q210684|lt=sangensha nagare-zukuri}} structure with {{ill|Wood shingle|Q199388|qid=Q199388}}, with a one-bay {{ill|kōhai|Q11415970|qid=Q11415970}} at the front. Built in the 12th year of {{ill|Eishō (Muromachi period)|Q1193577|qid=Q1193577}} ({{ill|1515|Q6208|qid=Q6208}}), it retains characteristics of the Muromachi period. In 1958 (Shōwa 33), it was designated a National {{ill|Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Q1188622|qid=Q1188622}}.

The treasure hall houses Important Cultural Properties such as a wooden standing statue of Shō Kannon, as well as ship ema and ship plaques designated as {{ill|National Important Tangible Folk Cultural Property|Q11644858|qid=Q11644858}}.

== Shrine grounds ==
The shrine grove, Oyama (the sacred mountain), is said to mark the northernmost habitat of the {{ill|Euterpnosia chibensis|Q5976326|qid=Q5976326}}, and in {{ill|1996|Q2070|qid=Q2070}} ({{ill|Heisei era|Q234510|qid=Q234510}} 8) it was selected as one of {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Japan’s 100 Soundscapes}}.

== Cultural properties ==
<small>(The designation type and date are shown in parentheses after each item.)</small>
;Important Cultural Properties (National)
* Main hall, with 4 ridge tags attached (structure, May 14, 1958 (Shōwa 33))
* Wooden standing statue of Shō Kannon, 1 figure (sculpture, April 14, {{ill|1906|Q2049|qid=Q2049}} (Meiji 39))
: A single-block carving of cherry wood, made in the late Heian period. Around the topknot on the head are traces indicating that faces like those seen on Eleven-Headed Kannon statues were once attached. At present, the arms from the shoulders onward are missing, and traces remain showing that multiple arms were once joined. However, the joints are too small for a Thousand-Armed Kannon, and it is presumed that the statue was originally created as an Eleven-Headed Kannon with four arms (two on each side). Eleven-Headed Kannon statues are usually two-armed, but among those created as the honji-butsu of Hakusan, there are examples with four arms.<ref>Special Exhibition Catalog, “Niigata Buddhist Sculpture Exhibition: Special Exhibition Commemorating the Recovery from the Chuetsu Earthquake,” Niigata Prefectural Museum of Modern Art, 2006, p.130</ref>
;Important Tangible Folk Cultural Properties (National)
* Maritime faith materials of Nou Hakusan Shrine, 97 items (March 3, 1987 (Shōwa 62))
: Includes ship ema and ship plaques. The ships depicted on the ema are called Hagase-bune.
;Important Intangible Folk Cultural Properties (National)
* Nou Bugaku (January 28, 1980 (Shōwa 55))
;Natural Monuments (National)
* Shrine grove of Nou Hakusan Shrine (December 21, 1937 (Shōwa 12))
* Habitat of the Nou Himeharu cicada (October 14, 1942 (Shōwa 17))

;Niigata Prefecture Designated Tangible Cultural Properties
* Bugaku masks, 4 pieces, with 1 additional piece (sculpture, March 27, 1981 (Shōwa 56))
* Bronze standing Eleven-Headed Kannon statue, 1 figure (sculpture, March 27, 1981 (Shōwa 56))
* Wooden seated statue of Taichō Daishi, 1 figure (sculpture, March 27, 1981 (Shōwa 56))
* Bronze temple bell, 1 piece (craft, March 31, 1976 (Shōwa 51))

;Itoigawa City Designated Tangible Cultural Properties
* Worship hall (structure, July 22, 1994 (Heisei 6))
* Group of Buddhist and Shinto statues, 43 figures (sculpture, May 12, 1972 (Shōwa 47))
* Ancient mirrors, 2 pieces (craft, May 12, 1972 (Shōwa 47))
* Complete Buddhist sutra written in gold on indigo paper, 1 scroll (calligraphy, May 12, 1972 (Shōwa 47))
* Vermilion-sealed documents of Tokugawa Iemitsu, 11 items (calligraphy, May 29, 1984 (Shōwa 59))
* Ridge tag, 1 piece (historical material, May 29, 1984 (Shōwa 59))
